explain.title: WHY?
lines: Soda is full of trapped CO2
Bubbles need a rough spot to start
A Mentos has countless tiny bumps

caption: Mentos + Diet Coke: everybody calls it a chemical reaction. It isn't. 🍬🥤 Same pH before and after: it's pure physics. What should we test next? 👇 #mentos #coke #physics #science #experiment #mythbusting #3danimation
description: Everyone has seen the Mentos and Diet Coke geyser, and most people think it's a chemical reaction. We drop rock salt into Diet Coke, then a Mentos, then measure what actually changed.

Rock salt gives a short fizz: about 1.0 s of reaction in the lab tests. A mint Mentos gives the famous geyser, lasting about 3.8 s. These durations come from a 2008 study by Tonya Coffey and her students at Appalachian State University, published in the American Journal of Physics.

It's not chemistry: the soda's pH was 3.0 before and 3.0 after, so nothing reacted. The CO2 is already dissolved in the soda and only needs a place to form bubbles. Under an atomic force microscope, a Mentos is covered in tiny bumps (rms roughness 442 nm, against 174 nm for rock salt). Each bump is a spot where bubbles can start, and the candy's coating makes bubbles even easier to form, so the gas escapes all at once.
The animation is a simulation: the geyser's shape and height are illustrative, the numbers on screen are the study's measurements.
sources_detail: T. S. Coffey, 'Diet Coke and Mentos: What is really behind this physical reaction?', American Journal of Physics 76, 551 (2008).
Measured: pH 3.0 before and after the Diet Coke + Mentos reaction (not acid/base). AFM rms roughness: mint Mentos 442 nm, rock salt 174 nm. Reaction duration: mint Mentos 3.8 s, rock salt 1.0 s.
Simulated: geyser height (about 2 m) and shape are illustrative, not measured.
